comments.text:
Great topic, when I was diagnosed with TRD they started adding personality disorder labels because I was still trying to get better.
It surprised me to learn that because I did not miss appointments I was labeled dependent personality trait. I was seeking relief.
And I did not know I was Autistic.

I was diagnosed with TRD and finally a new psychiatrist diagnosed me with ME Myalgic Encephalomyelitis. Then it has been a struggle as it is not a mood disorder I was back into my physicians care where not much is known. So it has been years of going through symptom by symptom getting assistance.
For over 13 years my main complaint was fatigue. Antidepressants did not work and I would even say harmed me as it took away all moods. 
Exercise made me worse. However because Post Exertional Malaise PEM or otherwise known as PENE Post Exertional Neuroimune Exhaustion happens 24 to 36 hours have the exertion. My crash was labeled as “fatigue is part of depression”.
Within months of my Autism diagnosis, I worked with my psychologist to communicate my fatigue with my psychiatrist and they listened. Changing my diagnosis to ME. 
I have since stopped pushing ie behaviour activation, exercise and practice radical rest and my mood has improved. 
It took me 3 years to withdrawal with supervision from all my antidepressants. 

I so agree the need to accept our conditions and circumstances yet if something does not feel quite right it needs addressing.
I went from surviving with TRD to thriving with ME. Yet from the outside I still look the same, only a few functional hours a day. Even that is expanding with the dysautonomia diagnosis and the hEDs diagnosis and learning to work with my body as it is today.

comments.text:
Podcasts like this are helping to push back against corruption within the pharmaceutical industry which is awesome to see. It’s also truly a breath of fresh air to hear Dr. Josef speak openly about the elephant in the room within psychiatry and how current practices may be negatively impacting people’s lives.
In my experience, antidepressants have felt like emotional numbing agents that take the life spark out of me, leaving me feeling disconnected and flattened emotionally. 
For some, it can even feel like a diminishing of one’s connection to soul or to God. That has been my personal experience as well.

I sincerely hope to see more companies and services open up to help patients safely come off these medications. There simply aren’t enough accessible options available, and the few that do exist are often too expensive or not covered by insurance, including Medicaid. It can feel as though the system is structured in a way that keeps individuals on medication long term on purpose.
As a result, many patients feel forced to become their own doctors and attempt to taper themselves, which is far from ideal. There needs to be more widely available, affordable support for those who want to discontinue their medications, including slower, more individualized tapering approaches than what is often taught in standard medical training. Additionally, the role and influence of the DSM-5 should be open to serious reconsideration and reform. Because as of right now most people on earth could be labeled with a mental illness according to the DSM-5. 
With that thanks for all you do for the community and keep doing what your doing. There are many people including myself who get so much out of these talks and greatly appreciate it. God bless you all. 🙏👍🏻🫶

I'm not fully through the video as of yet. But I have some things I'd like to say (about the video, and about myself). First of all, I think this is a GREAT thing to watch. Seeing how other people deal with their mental illnesses is so valuable! It helps people who might have mental illnesses realise theirs, or even realise there should not be any shame in it, and to seek help. And it helps those without to have more understanding.
Second of all, Beth seems like an awesome person. And I wanna thank her for being so open about her struggles! (And Buffy is the absolute best! I'd also be hard pressed to think what my favourite episode would be... I'll have to think on that for a bit)

I myself am diagnosed ASD (Autism Spectrum Disorder) and ADD. Both of which are very good at fucking up my life. ADD, surprisingly?, more so. And recently after chatting with a dear friend of mine, I have come to the realisation, that eventhough I have been taking medication for it for some time now (nearly a decade I think? since my diagnoses at any rate), I'm not finding it... effective or good enough. I take Bupropion, which is in it's essence a anti depressant. And I know that if I don't take it, I AM quite a bit more scatter brained and more high energy to the outside world. However, I have recently realised, I still HAVE all the issues that I had before I took the medication. It's just, only slightly milder. And at the time I accepted that as "well this is the best it'd gon' be". So my aim now is to get back to a psychiatrist, and try out a bunch of other meds that could help, to find the one that I DO find effective enough. And maybe, MAYBE, find one that will actually suppress the ADD enough that I might become the person I really would like to be.

comments.text: We think of our crossed over ones as far away. Nope. I've got a few of these small tap lamps around my living room. Normally I  tap them on the yellow warm light. When I last saw my mom in June last year (she lived at the coast I live inland), it was such an emotionally bonding time between me and my mom. On one occasion I told my mom you know how when a baby is born doctor has to snip the umbilical cord, it would be a bit awkward otherwise. I said well there's another cord, one you can't see, but God created it and runs straight from my soul to yours and nothing can break it. When I got home I hung up a painting from my grandfather's home I've always loved. I remembered I had one of my dad's favourite jerseys (he crossed over when I was 6. He crossed over on Father's Day which to me is a sign he was ready to leave this world). I washed that jersey, bought a great big teddy bear, who now wears my dad's jersey and is sat in a comfy chair looking at that painting that was part of his childhood too. I had two of these touch lamps on a shelf behind him, they're a sort of mushroom shape. Ever since they I put the teddy with his jersey on, these touch lamps would turn on randomly at about 2am. One morning just as I was about to leave for work, I tapped them off and asked out loud dad is it you playing with these lamps at 2am!? Ping the one on the right turned on. I moved them. One is in the kitchen unplugged, the other on a small round table. It randomly changes from the yellow light to the white light setting. The other evening it went off so I said out aloud OK, you turned it off, can you turn it back on. Ping it turned on. I've another two in the corner next to my small sofa. I woke up around midnight as if I'd had a solid 8 hours sleep, one of the ones in the corner turned to the white light setting from the yellow. Just now the one mushroom one went off, I said out loud, OK can you turn it back on please. I carried on watching your video and randomly turned, it was on again. The two in the corner, the one randomly went to white light. After the mushroom shape one turned back on I asked aloud, OK, now I asked aloud OK, now I don't know if it's you Poppy (her nickname and she crossed over on 2 January this year) or dad or both of you. Ping it turned immediately to the white light... A few nights after my mom crossed over, I turned my dvd off. I know it was off cause one of my doggies chewed the remote up so you physically have to  push a button to turn it off. I turned the TV off and as I turned to switch off another ordinary lamp the dvd player turned itself back on...

So true what you said about Bipolar having overlap with other disorders.

My AuDHD was mistaken for Bipolar as a kid and the antipsychotics and mood stabilizers didn’t help and only emptied my brain and personality.

It never goes into truly delusional or dangerous things. But I do look visibly manic when I get excited while unmasking and I talk a mile a minute and won’t shut up. 😅

Getting the right medication is so tough and I am so happy that you seem to be doing well!

comments.text:
I love this interview. I’ve seen so many doctors over the years and my most ubiquitous diagnosis combo has been Bipolar 2 and ADHD, which recent therapy has been uncovering could be cPTSD.

I can recall my first major medication reaction was akathisia in response to a mood stabilizer in grade school. I think it was in combination with ritalin but I may have been on adderall by that time. I wound up ripping my clothes off and “climbing the walls” by my parents’ recollection. Dad wound up tossing me out the back door in my underwear because he was exhausted and just wanted to get me to school and go to work.

My late mother’s records have been extremely helpful in identifying and understanding my psych history.

Thanks for sharing this beautiful exchange.

comments.text: I struggled my whole life, assuming that the high demand parenting I had experienced along with constant moving around the country, had caused my mental health issues.  However, from age 2, my parents were told I might have MS as I fainted regularly, went blind in one eye at age 10, had DAILY many multiple events of dizziness and partial  blindness through into my 40s.  Migraines, anxiety, fears, depression.  I had many female problems during that time including surgeries.   I had a partial hysterectomy at 41 and so was unaware that the escalation in symptoms were because it had spontaneously sent me into menopause.  At 50, I figured out that menopause was finished and went to my doctor for a confirmation blood test.  I requested several other tests as well and for some bizarre reason, requested a celiac test.  I discovered I had had celiac disease, my whole life!  No gluten meant dizziness, blindness issues, migraines, etc etc were all reduced dramatically, almost gone!  Even the emotional upheavals decreased!  It was then that I realized that my lovely but sad 12 year old son (who had never slept or ate well at all his whole life and had been mildly suicidal for several years) might be celiac as well!  Got him tested but he was negative.  I read about it and requested a biopsy.  He had the rashes, and many other non tummy issues.   Thank God the biopsy was done by a celiac specialist.  Instead of 1-3 spots taken as most doctors do, he took 15 and said nothing was suspicious until the last 3 spots.  Even then, he wasn't convinced except when he combined all the symptoms and so told us, 'Let's just call him celiac'.  Within 3 months, my son was no longer depressed, ate well and slept!  He is in his mid 20s now and we did get him therapy to unlearn bad thinking he had adopted while sick.  But he is extremely happy, lives across the country from us and is very successful in many ways.  You couldn't pay him, or me, to eat gluten on purpose and we neither one ever had the obvious tummy and bathroom issues!  We love therapy but now it accomplishes goals not just helping us survive that which doesn't seem to have explanation.  Celiac disease causes malnutrition!  Malnutrition affects our brains.  We are evidence of that.

comments.text: The label "treatment resistant depression" is not helpful for the client and, at worst, may cause harm by implying that getting better is hopeless. That said, "treatment resistant depression" is not a diagnosis. It is clinical shorthand for "hey, we've tried these interventions and they didn't work, so we'll need to go off the beaten path to see what's really going on here." While this language may be helpful for progress notes and for clinical consultation among providers, it's not language that should be (or is really meant to be) shared with the client, in my view. It's certainly not language that I would use with a client, at least. But I'm just a counselor in training, so take my opinion with a grain of salt.

comments.text:
Some of us are also hyper sensitive to progesteron (even the bioidentical kind). I am dealing with some hormone imbalances to the extent that my doctor put me on progesterone to try and get things sorted out, and usually progesterone HELPS with sleep. But for me, it woke me up every 15 minutes all night every night I took it and eventually tried taking it during the day which is not generally recommended because it’s supposed to make you sleepy, but we couldn’t think of another option- anyway the result was intense anxiety followed shortly by collapsing very suddenly on the floor unable to move my own limbs. I guess those of us with MTHFR just don’t respond to needed medicine in the usual way…..
I honestly think everyone should get a full MTHFR panel at this point. It seems to be behind a lot of the weird reactions and backwards responses to medication or stimulants. If your liver can’t methylate the help it’s being giving, the help isn’t going to hurt instead of help.

I'm going to lead with something that might sound like an attack (but I promise it isn't):  ADHD isn't real.
ADHD and dyslexia diagnoses are side effects of a collision between population growth, diminishing social value of the trades, and a severely outdated education system.
I don't know you at all, but I can tell that you're probably American from your accent, and probably an aesthete from your grooming style and choice of decor.  Cardboard box in frame is interesting...it's the only thing of its type.  Everything else is perfectly curated.  I would guess that you left it there for effect.
Nothing about you looks like depression.  If you are depressed, why do you exhibit no signs of it?  This isn't me doubting you.  This is me saying, if you are depressed, why are you masking?

You asked a question in response to someone else:  "Is a life worth living without being happy?"  I'm tempted to say "no", just because it breaks the illusion that it's an honest question.  Life's worth is entirely subjective to the individual experience.  If you require "happiness" to a certain level, and you feel your life is not at sufficient "happiness", you have to determine whether a path to the sufficient level exists, right?  This is the trap of depression.

Challenge the parameters.  Are you sure "happiness" is a good metric for determining life's worth?

THISSSS!!!! I could write a freakin' Book about all the professionals, medications, tests, exercises, therapies, spirituality practices, programs, hospitals, etc. I've tried in the last 10-11 years for depression, and it was only when *I* started to look into other disorders/illnesses when I found that my "depression" and "generalized anxiety" was actually 3 (and potentially more) undiagnosed illnesses in a trenchcoat! I just think back to all those times someone (with a professional degree!) could have noticed or inquired further, leading to any other factor, and I'm so bitter. The actual name of "treatment-resistant depression" didn't really bother me, it honestly kinda felt like validation that I've been trying but am still struggling (also I don't believe it's an official DSM term), but I really do wonder if doctors saw "treatment resistant depression" as "depression+" if they would be more inclined to step back and say "there's more to the story that we're missing". A fair amount of depression treatments involve symptom management, which while that has it's advantages, doesn't address the root cause(s). 

If anyone's been struggling with "treatment-resistant depression", your suffering and struggling is so fucking valid. You are not failing or a failure. I know you have worked so much harder at living and finding relief than anyone may ever give you credit for. I am so proud of you. ❤‍🩹❤‍🩹

comments.text:
Great topic, when I was diagnosed with TRD they started adding personality disorder labels because I was still trying to get better.
It surprised me to learn that because I did not miss appointments I was labeled dependent personality trait. I was seeking relief.
And I did not know I was Autistic.

I was diagnosed with TRD and finally a new psychiatrist diagnosed me with ME Myalgic Encephalomyelitis. Then it has been a struggle as it is not a mood disorder I was back into my physicians care where not much is known. So it has been years of going through symptom by symptom getting assistance.
For over 13 years my main complaint was fatigue. Antidepressants did not work and I would even say harmed me as it took away all moods. 
Exercise made me worse. However because Post Exertional Malaise PEM or otherwise known as PENE Post Exertional Neuroimune Exhaustion happens 24 to 36 hours have the exertion. My crash was labeled as “fatigue is part of depression”.
Within months of my Autism diagnosis, I worked with my psychologist to communicate my fatigue with my psychiatrist and they listened. Changing my diagnosis to ME. 
I have since stopped pushing ie behaviour activation, exercise and practice radical rest and my mood has improved. 
It took me 3 years to withdrawal with supervision from all my antidepressants. 

I so agree the need to accept our conditions and circumstances yet if something does not feel quite right it needs addressing.
I went from surviving with TRD to thriving with ME. Yet from the outside I still look the same, only a few functional hours a day. Even that is expanding with the dysautonomia diagnosis and the hEDs diagnosis and learning to work with my body as it is today.

comments.text:
Podcasts like this are helping to push back against corruption within the pharmaceutical industry which is awesome to see. It’s also truly a breath of fresh air to hear Dr. Josef speak openly about the elephant in the room within psychiatry and how current practices may be negatively impacting people’s lives.
In my experience, antidepressants have felt like emotional numbing agents that take the life spark out of me, leaving me feeling disconnected and flattened emotionally. 
For some, it can even feel like a diminishing of one’s connection to soul or to God. That has been my personal experience as well.

I sincerely hope to see more companies and services open up to help patients safely come off these medications. There simply aren’t enough accessible options available, and the few that do exist are often too expensive or not covered by insurance, including Medicaid. It can feel as though the system is structured in a way that keeps individuals on medication long term on purpose.
As a result, many patients feel forced to become their own doctors and attempt to taper themselves, which is far from ideal. There needs to be more widely available, affordable support for those who want to discontinue their medications, including slower, more individualized tapering approaches than what is often taught in standard medical training. Additionally, the role and influence of the DSM-5 should be open to serious reconsideration and reform. Because as of right now most people on earth could be labeled with a mental illness according to the DSM-5. 
With that thanks for all you do for the community and keep doing what your doing. There are many people including myself who get so much out of these talks and greatly appreciate it. God bless you all. 🙏👍🏻🫶

I'm not fully through the video as of yet. But I have some things I'd like to say (about the video, and about myself). First of all, I think this is a GREAT thing to watch. Seeing how other people deal with their mental illnesses is so valuable! It helps people who might have mental illnesses realise theirs, or even realise there should not be any shame in it, and to seek help. And it helps those without to have more understanding.
Second of all, Beth seems like an awesome person. And I wanna thank her for being so open about her struggles! (And Buffy is the absolute best! I'd also be hard pressed to think what my favourite episode would be... I'll have to think on that for a bit)

I myself am diagnosed ASD (Autism Spectrum Disorder) and ADD. Both of which are very good at fucking up my life. ADD, surprisingly?, more so. And recently after chatting with a dear friend of mine, I have come to the realisation, that eventhough I have been taking medication for it for some time now (nearly a decade I think? since my diagnoses at any rate), I'm not finding it... effective or good enough. I take Bupropion, which is in it's essence a anti depressant. And I know that if I don't take it, I AM quite a bit more scatter brained and more high energy to the outside world. However, I have recently realised, I still HAVE all the issues that I had before I took the medication. It's just, only slightly milder. And at the time I accepted that as "well this is the best it'd gon' be". So my aim now is to get back to a psychiatrist, and try out a bunch of other meds that could help, to find the one that I DO find effective enough. And maybe, MAYBE, find one that will actually suppress the ADD enough that I might become the person I really would like to be.

comments.text: We think of our crossed over ones as far away. Nope. I've got a few of these small tap lamps around my living room. Normally I  tap them on the yellow warm light. When I last saw my mom in June last year (she lived at the coast I live inland), it was such an emotionally bonding time between me and my mom. On one occasion I told my mom you know how when a baby is born doctor has to snip the umbilical cord, it would be a bit awkward otherwise. I said well there's another cord, one you can't see, but God created it and runs straight from my soul to yours and nothing can break it. When I got home I hung up a painting from my grandfather's home I've always loved. I remembered I had one of my dad's favourite jerseys (he crossed over when I was 6. He crossed over on Father's Day which to me is a sign he was ready to leave this world). I washed that jersey, bought a great big teddy bear, who now wears my dad's jersey and is sat in a comfy chair looking at that painting that was part of his childhood too. I had two of these touch lamps on a shelf behind him, they're a sort of mushroom shape. Ever since they I put the teddy with his jersey on, these touch lamps would turn on randomly at about 2am. One morning just as I was about to leave for work, I tapped them off and asked out loud dad is it you playing with these lamps at 2am!? Ping the one on the right turned on. I moved them. One is in the kitchen unplugged, the other on a small round table. It randomly changes from the yellow light to the white light setting. The other evening it went off so I said out aloud OK, you turned it off, can you turn it back on. Ping it turned on. I've another two in the corner next to my small sofa. I woke up around midnight as if I'd had a solid 8 hours sleep, one of the ones in the corner turned to the white light setting from the yellow. My late mother’s records have been extremely helpful in identifying and understanding my psych history.

comments.text: I struggled my whole life, assuming that the high demand parenting I had experienced along with constant moving around the country, had caused my mental health issues.  However, from age 2, my parents were told I might have MS as I fainted regularly, went blind in one eye at age 10, had DAILY many multiple events of dizziness and partial  blindness through into my 40s.  Migraines, anxiety, fears, depression.  I had many female problems during that time including surgeries.   I had a partial hysterectomy at 41 and so was unaware that the escalation in symptoms were because it had spontaneously sent me into menopause.  At 50, I figured out that menopause was finished and went to my doctor for a confirmation blood test.  I requested several other tests as well and for some bizarre reason, requested a celiac test.  I discovered I had had celiac disease, my whole life!  No gluten meant dizziness, blindness issues, migraines, etc etc were all reduced dramatically, almost gone!  Even the emotional upheavals decreased!  It was then that I realized that my lovely but sad 12 year old son (who had never slept or ate well at all his whole life and had been mildly suicidal for several years) might be celiac as well!  Got him tested but he was negative.  I read about it and requested a biopsy.  He had the rashes, and many other non tummy issues.   Thank God the biopsy was done by a celiac specialist.  Instead of 1-3 spots taken as most doctors do, he took 15 and said nothing was suspicious until the last 3 spots.  Even then, he wasn't convinced except when he combined all the symptoms and so told us, 'Let's just call him celiac'.  Within 3 months, my son was no longer depressed, ate well and slept!  He is in his mid 20s now and we did get him therapy to unlearn bad thinking he had adopted while sick.  But he is extremely happy, lives across the country from us and is very successful in many ways.  You couldn't pay him, or me, to eat gluten on purpose and we neither one ever had the obvious tummy and bathroom issues!  We love therapy but now it accomplishes goals not just helping us survive that which doesn't seem to have explanation.  Celiac disease causes malnutrition!  Malnutrition affects our brains.  We are evidence of that.

comments.text: The label "treatment resistant depression" is not helpful for the client and, at worst, may cause harm by implying that getting better is hopeless. That said, "treatment resistant depression" is not a diagnosis. It is clinical shorthand for "hey, we've tried these interventions and they didn't work, so we'll need to go off the beaten path to see what's really going on here." While this language may be helpful for progress notes and for clinical consultation among providers, it's not language that should be (or is really meant to be) shared with the client, in my view. It's certainly not language that I would use with a client, at least. But I'm just a counselor in training, so take my opinion with a grain of salt.

Some of us are also hyper sensitive to progesteron (even the bioidentical kind). I am dealing with some hormone imbalances to the extent that my doctor put me on progesterone to try and get things sorted out, and usually progesterone HELPS with sleep. But for me, it woke me up every 15 minutes all night every night I took it and eventually tried taking it during the day which is not generally recommended because it’s supposed to make you sleepy, but we couldn’t think of another option- anyway the result was intense anxiety followed shortly by collapsing very suddenly on the floor unable to move my own limbs. I guess those of us with MTHFR just don’t respond to needed medicine in the usual way…..
I honestly think everyone should get a full MTHFR panel at this point. It seems to be behind a lot of the weird reactions and backwards responses to medication or stimulants. If your liver can’t methylate the help it’s being giving, the help isn’t going to hurt instead of help.

I'm going to lead with something that might sound like an attack (but I promise it isn't):  ADHD isn't real.
ADHD and dyslexia diagnoses are side effects of a collision between population growth, diminishing social value of the trades, and a severely outdated education system.
I don't know you at all, but I can tell that you're probably American from your accent, and probably an aesthete from your grooming style and choice of decor.  Cardboard box in frame is interesting...it's the only thing of its type.  Everything else is perfectly curated.  I would guess that you left it there for effect.
Nothing about you looks like depression.  If you are depressed, why do you exhibit no signs of it?  This isn't me doubting you.  This is me saying, if you are depressed, why are you masking?

You asked a question in response to someone else:  "Is a life worth living without being happy?"  I'm tempted to say "no", just because it breaks the illusion that it's an honest question.  Life's worth is entirely subjective to the individual experience.  If you require "happiness" to a certain level, and you feel your life is not at sufficient "happiness", you have to determine whether a path to the sufficient level exists, right?  This is the trap of depression.

Challenge the parameters.  Are you sure "happiness" is a good metric for determining life's worth?

comments.text:
THISSSS!!!! I could write a freakin' Book about all the professionals, medications, tests, exercises, therapies, spirituality practices, programs, hospitals, etc. I've tried in the last 10-11 years for depression, and it was only when *I* started to look into other disorders/illnesses when I found that my "depression" and "generalized anxiety" was actually 3 (and potentially more) undiagnosed illnesses in a trenchcoat! I just think back to all those times someone (with a professional degree!) could have noticed or inquired further, leading to any other factor, and I'm so bitter. The actual name of "treatment-resistant depression" didn't really bother me, it honestly kinda felt like validation that I've been trying but am still struggling (also I don't believe it's an official DSM term), but I really do wonder if doctors saw "treatment resistant depression" as "depression+" if they would be more inclined to step back and say "there's more to the story that we're missing". A fair amount of depression treatments involve symptom management, which while that has it's advantages, doesn't address the root cause(s). 

If anyone's been struggling with "treatment-resistant depression", your suffering and struggling is so fucking valid. You are not failing or a failure. I know you have worked so much harder at living and finding relief than anyone may ever give you credit for. I am so proud of you. ❤‍🩹❤‍🩹

Great topic, when I was diagnosed with TRD they started adding personality disorder labels because I was still trying to get better.
It surprised me to learn that because I did not miss appointments I was labeled dependent personality trait. I was seeking relief.
And I did not know I was Autistic.

I was diagnosed with TRD and finally a new psychiatrist diagnosed me with ME Myalgic Encephalomyelitis. Then it has been a struggle as it is not a mood disorder I was back into my physicians care where not much is known. So it has been years of going through symptom by symptom getting assistance.
For over 13 years my main complaint was fatigue. Antidepressants did not work and I would even say harmed me as it took away all moods. 
Exercise made me worse. However because Post Exertional Malaise PEM or otherwise known as PENE Post Exertional Neuroimune Exhaustion happens 24 to 36 hours have the exertion. My crash was labeled as “fatigue is part of depression”.
Within months of my Autism diagnosis, I worked with my psychologist to communicate my fatigue with my psychiatrist and they listened. Changing my diagnosis to ME. 
I have since stopped pushing ie behaviour activation, exercise and practice radical rest and my mood has improved. 
It took me 3 years to withdrawal with supervision from all my antidepressants. 

I so agree the need to accept our conditions and circumstances yet if something does not feel quite right it needs addressing.
I went from surviving with TRD to thriving with ME. Yet from the outside I still look the same, only a few functional hours a day. Even that is expanding with the dysautonomia diagnosis and the hEDs diagnosis and learning to work with my body as it is today.

comments.text:
Podcasts like this are helping to push back against corruption within the pharmaceutical industry which is awesome to see. It’s also truly a breath of fresh air to hear Dr. Josef speak openly about the elephant in the room within psychiatry and how current practices may be negatively impacting people’s lives.
In my experience, antidepressants have felt like emotional numbing agents that take the life spark out of me, leaving me feeling disconnected and flattened emotionally. 
For some, it can even feel like a diminishing of one’s connection to soul or to God. That has been my personal experience as well.

I sincerely hope to see more companies and services open up to help patients safely come off these medications. There simply aren’t enough accessible options available, and the few that do exist are often too expensive or not covered by insurance, including Medicaid. It can feel as though the system is structured in a way that keeps individuals on medication long term on purpose.
As a result, many patients feel forced to become their own doctors and attempt to taper themselves, which is far from ideal. There needs to be more widely available, affordable support for those who want to discontinue their medications, including slower, more individualized tapering approaches than what is often taught in standard medical training. Additionally, the role and influence of the DSM-5 should be open to serious reconsideration and reform. Because as of right now most people on earth could be labeled with a mental illness according to the DSM-5. 
With that thanks for all you do for the community and keep doing what your doing. There are many people including myself who get so much out of these talks and greatly appreciate it. God bless you all. 🙏👍🏻🫶

I'm not fully through the video as of yet. But I have some things I'd like to say (about the video, and about myself). First of all, I think this is a GREAT thing to watch. Seeing how other people deal with their mental illnesses is so valuable! It helps people who might have mental illnesses realise theirs, or even realise there should not be any shame in it, and to seek help. And it helps those without to have more understanding.
Second of all, Beth seems like an awesome person. And I wanna thank her for being so open about her struggles! (And Buffy is the absolute best! I'd also be hard pressed to think what my favourite episode would be... I'll have to think on that for a bit)

I myself am diagnosed ASD (Autism Spectrum Disorder) and ADD. Both of which are very good at fucking up my life. ADD, surprisingly?, more so. And recently after chatting with a dear friend of mine, I have come to the realisation, that eventhough I have been taking medication for it for some time now (nearly a decade I think? since my diagnoses at any rate), I'm not finding it... effective or good enough. I take Bupropion, which is in it's essence a anti depressant. And I know that if I don't take it, I AM quite a bit more scatter brained and more high energy to the outside world. However, I have recently realised, I still HAVE all the issues that I had before I took the medication. It's just, only slightly milder. And at the time I accepted that as "well this is the best it'd gon' be". So my aim now is to get back to a psychiatrist, and try out a bunch of other meds that could help, to find the one that I DO find effective enough. And maybe, MAYBE, find one that will actually suppress the ADD enough that I might become the person I really would like to be.


This time, NOT ONLY FOR THE ALGORITHM, THIS TIME I'M ACTUALLY SAYING SOMETHING!!!! WHOOOOO

When I last saw my mom in June last year (she lived at the coast I live inland), it was such an emotionally bonding time between me and my mom. On one occasion I told my mom you know how when a baby is born doctor has to snip the umbilical cord, it would be a bit awkward otherwise. I said well there's another cord, one you can't see, but God created it and runs straight from my soul to yours and nothing can break it. When I got home I hung up a painting from my grandfather's home I've always loved. I remembered I had one of my dad's favourite jerseys (he crossed over when I was 6. I washed that jersey, bought a great big teddy bear, who now wears my dad's jersey and is sat in a comfy chair looking at that painting that was part of his childhood too. I had two of these touch lamps on a shelf behind him, they're a sort of mushroom shape. Ever since they I put the teddy with his jersey on, these touch lamps would turn on randomly at about 2am. One morning just as I was about to leave for work, I tapped them off and asked out loud dad is it you playing with these lamps at 2am!? Ping the one on the right turned on. I moved them. The other evening it went off so I said out aloud OK, you turned it off, can you turn it back on. Ping it turned on. I've another two in the corner next to my small sofa. I love this interview. I’ve seen so many doctors over the years and my most ubiquitous diagnosis combo has been Bipolar 2 and ADHD, which recent therapy has been uncovering could be cPTSD.

I can recall my first major medication reaction was akathisia in response to a mood stabilizer in grade school. I think it was in combination with ritalin but I may have been on adderall by that time. I wound up ripping my clothes off and “climbing the walls” by my parents’ recollection. Dad wound up tossing me out the back door in my underwear because he was exhausted and just wanted to get me to school and go to work.

My late mother’s records have been extremely helpful in identifying and understanding my psych history.

Thanks for sharing this beautiful exchange.

comments.text: I struggled my whole life, assuming that the high demand parenting I had experienced along with constant moving around the country, had caused my mental health issues.  However, from age 2, my parents were told I might have MS as I fainted regularly, went blind in one eye at age 10, had DAILY many multiple events of dizziness and partial  blindness through into my 40s.  Migraines, anxiety, fears, depression.  I had many female problems during that time including surgeries.   I had a partial hysterectomy at 41 and so was unaware that the escalation in symptoms were because it had spontaneously sent me into menopause.  At 50, I figured out that menopause was finished and went to my doctor for a confirmation blood test.  I requested several other tests as well and for some bizarre reason, requested a celiac test.  I discovered I had had celiac disease, my whole life!  No gluten meant dizziness, blindness issues, migraines, etc etc were all reduced dramatically, almost gone!  Even the emotional upheavals decreased!  It was then that I realized that my lovely but sad 12 year old son (who had never slept or ate well at all his whole life and had been mildly suicidal for several years) might be celiac as well!  Got him tested but he was negative.  I read about it and requested a biopsy.  He had the rashes, and many other non tummy issues.   Thank God the biopsy was done by a celiac specialist.  Instead of 1-3 spots taken as most doctors do, he took 15 and said nothing was suspicious until the last 3 spots.  Even then, he wasn't convinced except when he combined all the symptoms and so told us, 'Let's just call him celiac'.  Within 3 months, my son was no longer depressed, ate well and slept!  He is in his mid 20s now and we did get him therapy to unlearn bad thinking he had adopted while sick.  But he is extremely happy, lives across the country from us and is very successful in many ways.  You couldn't pay him, or me, to eat gluten on purpose and we neither one ever had the obvious tummy and bathroom issues!  We love therapy but now it accomplishes goals not just helping us survive that which doesn't seem to have explanation.  Celiac disease causes malnutrition!  Malnutrition affects our brains.  We are evidence of that.

comments.text: The label "treatment resistant depression" is not helpful for the client and, at worst, may cause harm by implying that getting better is hopeless. That said, "treatment resistant depression" is not a diagnosis. It is clinical shorthand for "hey, we've tried these interventions and they didn't work, so we'll need to go off the beaten path to see what's really going on here." While this language may be helpful for progress notes and for clinical consultation among providers, it's not language that should be (or is really meant to be) shared with the client, in my view. It's certainly not language that I would use with a client, at least. But I'm just a counselor in training, so take my opinion with a grain of salt.

I'm going to lead with something that might sound like an attack (but I promise it isn't):  ADHD isn't real.
ADHD and dyslexia diagnoses are side effects of a collision between population growth, diminishing social value of the trades, and a severely outdated education system.
I don't know you at all, but I can tell that you're probably American from your accent, and probably an aesthete from your grooming style and choice of decor.  Cardboard box in frame is interesting...it's the only thing of its type.  Everything else is perfectly curated.  I would guess that you left it there for effect.
Nothing about you looks like depression.  If you are depressed, why do you exhibit no signs of it?  This isn't me doubting you.  This is me saying, if you are depressed, why are you masking?

You asked a question in response to someone else:  "Is a life worth living without being happy?"  I'm tempted to say "no", just because it breaks the illusion that it's an honest question.  Life's worth is entirely subjective to the individual experience.  If you require "happiness" to a certain level, and you feel your life is not at sufficient "happiness", you have to determine whether a path to the sufficient level exists, right?  This is the trap of depression.

Challenge the parameters.  Are you sure "happiness" is a good metric for determining life's worth?

THISSSS!!!! I could write a freakin' Book about all the professionals, medications, tests, exercises, therapies, spirituality practices, programs, hospitals, etc. I've tried in the last 10-11 years for depression, and it was only when *I* started to look into other disorders/illnesses when I found that my "depression" and "generalized anxiety" was actually 3 (and potentially more) undiagnosed illnesses in a trenchcoat! I just think back to all those times someone (with a professional degree!) could have noticed or inquired further, leading to any other factor, and I'm so bitter. The actual name of "treatment-resistant depression" didn't really bother me, it honestly kinda felt like validation that I've been trying but am still struggling (also I don't believe it's an official DSM term), but I really do wonder if doctors saw "treatment resistant depression" as "depression+" if they would be more inclined to step back and say "there's more to the story that we're missing". A fair amount of depression treatments involve symptom management, which while that has it's advantages, doesn't address the root cause(s). 

If anyone's been struggling with "treatment-resistant depression", your suffering and struggling is so fucking valid. You are not failing or a failure. I know you have worked so much harder at living and finding relief than anyone may ever give you credit for. I am so proud of you. ❤‍🩹❤‍🩹

comments.text:
Great topic, when I was diagnosed with TRD they started adding personality disorder labels because I was still trying to get better.
It surprised me to learn that because I did not miss appointments I was labeled dependent personality trait. I was seeking relief.
And I did not know I was Autistic.

I was diagnosed with TRD and finally a new psychiatrist diagnosed me with ME Myalgic Encephalomyelitis. Then it has been a struggle as it is not a mood disorder I was back into my physicians care where not much is known. So it has been years of going through symptom by symptom getting assistance.
For over 13 years my main complaint was fatigue. Antidepressants did not work and I would even say harmed me as it took away all moods. 
Exercise made me worse. However because Post Exertional Malaise PEM or otherwise known as PENE Post Exertional Neuroimune Exhaustion happens 24 to 36 hours have the exertion. My crash was labeled as “fatigue is part of depression”.
Within months of my Autism diagnosis, I worked with my psychologist to communicate my fatigue with my psychiatrist and they listened. Changing my diagnosis to ME. 
I have since stopped pushing ie behaviour activation, exercise and practice radical rest and my mood has improved. 
It took me 3 years to withdrawal with supervision from all my antidepressants. 

I so agree the need to accept our conditions and circumstances yet if something does not feel quite right it needs addressing.
I went from surviving with TRD to thriving with ME. Yet from the outside I still look the same, only a few functional hours a day. Even that is expanding with the dysautonomia diagnosis and the hEDs diagnosis and learning to work with my body as it is today.

comments.text:
Podcasts like this are helping to push back against corruption within the pharmaceutical industry which is awesome to see. It’s also truly a breath of fresh air to hear Dr. Josef speak openly about the elephant in the room within psychiatry and how current practices may be negatively impacting people’s lives.
In my experience, antidepressants have felt like emotional numbing agents that take the life spark out of me, leaving me feeling disconnected and flattened emotionally. 
For some, it can even feel like a diminishing of one’s connection to soul or to God. That has been my personal experience as well.

I sincerely hope to see more companies and services open up to help patients safely come off these medications. There simply aren’t enough accessible options available, and the few that do exist are often too expensive or not covered by insurance, including Medicaid. It can feel as though the system is structured in a way that keeps individuals on medication long term on purpose.
As a result, many patients feel forced to become their own doctors and attempt to taper themselves, which is far from ideal. There needs to be more widely available, affordable support for those who want to discontinue their medications, including slower, more individualized tapering approaches than what is often taught in standard medical training. Additionally, the role and influence of the DSM-5 should be open to serious reconsideration and reform. Because as of right now most people on earth could be labeled with a mental illness according to the DSM-5. 
With that thanks for all you do for the community and keep doing what your doing. There are many people including myself who get so much out of these talks and greatly appreciate it. God bless you all. 🙏👍🏻🫶

I'm not fully through the video as of yet. But I have some things I'd like to say (about the video, and about myself). First of all, I think this is a GREAT thing to watch. Seeing how other people deal with their mental illnesses is so valuable! It helps people who might have mental illnesses realise theirs, or even realise there should not be any shame in it, and to seek help. And it helps those without to have more understanding.
Second of all, Beth seems like an awesome person. And I wanna thank her for being so open about her struggles! (And Buffy is the absolute best! I'd also be hard pressed to think what my favourite episode would be... I'll have to think on that for a bit)

I myself am diagnosed ASD (Autism Spectrum Disorder) and ADD. Both of which are very good at fucking up my life. ADD, surprisingly?, more so. And recently after chatting with a dear friend of mine, I have come to the realisation, that eventhough I have been taking medication for it for some time now (nearly a decade I think? since my diagnoses at any rate), I'm not finding it... effective or good enough. I take Bupropion, which is in it's essence a anti depressant. And I know that if I don't take it, I AM quite a bit more scatter brained and more high energy to the outside world. However, I have recently realised, I still HAVE all the issues that I had before I took the medication. It's just, only slightly milder. And at the time I accepted that as "well this is the best it'd gon' be". So my aim now is to get back to a psychiatrist, and try out a bunch of other meds that could help, to find the one that I DO find effective enough. And maybe, MAYBE, find one that will actually suppress the ADD enough that I might become the person I really would like to be.

comments.text: I struggled my whole life, assuming that the high demand parenting I had experienced along with constant moving around the country, had caused my mental health issues.  However, from age 2, my parents were told I might have MS as I fainted regularly, went blind in one eye at age 10, had DAILY many multiple events of dizziness and partial  blindness through into my 40s.  Migraines, anxiety, fears, depression.  I had many female problems during that time including surgeries.   I had a partial hysterectomy at 41 and so was unaware that the escalation in symptoms were because it had spontaneously sent me into menopause.  At 50, I figured out that menopause was finished and went to my doctor for a confirmation blood test.  I requested several other tests as well and for some bizarre reason, requested a celiac test.  I discovered I had had celiac disease, my whole life!  No gluten meant dizziness, blindness issues, migraines, etc etc were all reduced dramatically, almost gone!  Even the emotional upheavals decreased!  It was then that I realized that my lovely but sad 12 year old son (who had never slept or ate well at all his whole life and had been mildly suicidal for several years) might be celiac as well!  Got him tested but he was negative.  I read about it and requested a biopsy.  He had the rashes, and many other non tummy issues.   Thank God the biopsy was done by a celiac specialist.  Instead of 1-3 spots taken as most doctors do, he took 15 and said nothing was suspicious until the last 3 spots.  Even then, he wasn't convinced except when he combined all the symptoms and so told us, 'Let's just call him celiac'.  Within 3 months, my son was no longer depressed, ate well and slept!  He is in his mid 20s now and we did get him therapy to unlearn bad thinking he had adopted while sick.  But he is extremely happy, lives across the country from us and is very successful in many ways.  You couldn't pay him, or me, to eat gluten on purpose and we neither one ever had the obvious tummy and bathroom issues!  We love therapy but now it accomplishes goals not just helping us survive that which doesn't seem to have explanation.  Celiac disease causes malnutrition!  Malnutrition affects our brains.  We are evidence of that.

comments.text: The label "treatment resistant depression" is not helpful for the client and, at worst, may cause harm by implying that getting better is hopeless. That said, "treatment resistant depression" is not a diagnosis. It is clinical shorthand for "hey, we've tried these interventions and they didn't work, so we'll need to go off the beaten path to see what's really going on here." While this language may be helpful for progress notes and for clinical consultation among providers, it's not language that should be (or is really meant to be) shared with the client, in my view. It's certainly not language that I would use with a client, at least. But I'm just a counselor in training, so take my opinion with a grain of salt.

Some of us are also hyper sensitive to progesteron (even the bioidentical kind). I am dealing with some hormone imbalances to the extent that my doctor put me on progesterone to try and get things sorted out, and usually progesterone HELPS with sleep. But for me, it woke me up every 15 minutes all night every night I took it and eventually tried taking it during the day which is not generally recommended because it’s supposed to make you sleepy, but we couldn’t think of another option- anyway the result was intense anxiety followed shortly by collapsing very suddenly on the floor unable to move my own limbs. I guess those of us with MTHFR just don’t respond to needed medicine in the usual way…..
I honestly think everyone should get a full MTHFR panel at this point. It seems to be behind a lot of the weird reactions and backwards responses to medication or stimulants. If your liver can’t methylate the help it’s being giving, the help isn’t going to hurt instead of help.

I'm going to lead with something that might sound like an attack (but I promise it isn't):  ADHD isn't real.
ADHD and dyslexia diagnoses are side effects of a collision between population growth, diminishing social value of the trades, and a severely outdated education system.
I don't know you at all, but I can tell that you're probably American from your accent, and probably an aesthete from your grooming style and choice of decor.  Cardboard box in frame is interesting...it's the only thing of its type.  Everything else is perfectly curated.  I would guess that you left it there for effect.
Nothing about you looks like depression.  If you are depressed, why do you exhibit no signs of it?  This isn't me doubting you.  This is me saying, if you are depressed, why are you masking?

You asked a question in response to someone else:  "Is a life worth living without being happy?"  I'm tempted to say "no", just because it breaks the illusion that it's an honest question.  Life's worth is entirely subjective to the individual experience.  If you require "happiness" to a certain level, and you feel your life is not at sufficient "happiness", you have to determine whether a path to the sufficient level exists, right?  This is the trap of depression.

Challenge the parameters.  Are you sure "happiness" is a good metric for determining life's worth?

comments.text:
THISSSS!!!! I could write a freakin' Book about all the professionals, medications, tests, exercises, therapies, spirituality practices, programs, hospitals, etc. I've tried in the last 10-11 years for depression, and it was only when *I* started to look into other disorders/illnesses when I found that my "depression" and "generalized anxiety" was actually 3 (and potentially more) undiagnosed illnesses in a trenchcoat! I just think back to all those times someone (with a professional degree!) could have noticed or inquired further, leading to any other factor, and I'm so bitter. The actual name of "treatment-resistant depression" didn't really bother me, it honestly kinda felt like validation that I've been trying but am still struggling (also I don't believe it's an official DSM term), but I really do wonder if doctors saw "treatment resistant depression" as "depression+" if they would be more inclined to step back and say "there's more to the story that we're missing". A fair amount of depression treatments involve symptom management, which while that has it's advantages, doesn't address the root cause(s). 

If anyone's been struggling with "treatment-resistant depression", your suffering and struggling is so fucking valid. You are not failing or a failure. I know you have worked so much harder at living and finding relief than anyone may ever give you credit for. I am so proud of you. ❤‍🩹❤‍🩹

comments.text:
Great topic, when I was diagnosed with TRD they started adding personality disorder labels because I was still trying to get better.
It surprised me to learn that because I did not miss appointments I was labeled dependent personality trait. I was seeking relief.
And I did not know I was Autistic.

I was diagnosed with TRD and finally a new psychiatrist diagnosed me with ME Myalgic Encephalomyelitis. Then it has been a struggle as it is not a mood disorder I was back into my physicians care where not much is known. So it has been years of going through symptom by symptom getting assistance.
For over 13 years my main complaint was fatigue. Antidepressants did not work and I would even say harmed me as it took away all moods. 
Exercise made me worse. However because Post Exertional Malaise PEM or otherwise known as PENE Post Exertional Neuroimune Exhaustion happens 24 to 36 hours have the exertion. My crash was labeled as “fatigue is part of depression”.
Within months of my Autism diagnosis, I worked with my psychologist to communicate my fatigue with my psychiatrist and they listened. Changing my diagnosis to ME. 
I have since stopped pushing ie behaviour activation, exercise and practice radical rest and my mood has improved. 
It took me 3 years to withdrawal with supervision from all my antidepressants. 

I so agree the need to accept our conditions and circumstances yet if something does not feel quite right it needs addressing.

comments.text:
Podcasts like this are helping to push back against corruption within the pharmaceutical industry which is awesome to see. It’s also truly a breath of fresh air to hear Dr. Josef speak openly about the elephant in the room within psychiatry and how current practices may be negatively impacting people’s lives.
In my experience, antidepressants have felt like emotional numbing agents that take the life spark out of me, leaving me feeling disconnected and flattened emotionally. 
For some, it can even feel like a diminishing of one’s connection to soul or to God. That has been my personal experience as well.

I sincerely hope to see more companies and services open up to help patients safely come off these medications. There simply aren’t enough accessible options available, and the few that do exist are often too expensive or not covered by insurance, including Medicaid. It can feel as though the system is structured in a way that keeps individuals on medication long term on purpose.
As a result, many patients feel forced to become their own doctors and attempt to taper themselves, which is far from ideal. There needs to be more widely available, affordable support for those who want to discontinue their medications, including slower, more individualized tapering approaches than what is often taught in standard medical training. Additionally, the role and influence of the DSM-5 should be open to serious reconsideration and reform. Because as of right now most people on earth could be labeled with a mental illness according to the DSM-5. 
With that thanks for all you do for the community and keep doing what your doing. There are many people including myself who get so much out of these talks and greatly appreciate it. God bless you all. 🙏👍🏻🫶

I'm not fully through the video as of yet. But I have some things I'd like to say (about the video, and about myself). First of all, I think this is a GREAT thing to watch. Seeing how other people deal with their mental illnesses is so valuable! It helps people who might have mental illnesses realise theirs, or even realise there should not be any shame in it, and to seek help. And it helps those without to have more understanding.
Second of all, Beth seems like an awesome person. And I wanna thank her for being so open about her struggles! (And Buffy is the absolute best! I'd also be hard pressed to think what my favourite episode would be... I'll have to think on that for a bit)

I myself am diagnosed ASD (Autism Spectrum Disorder) and ADD. Both of which are very good at fucking up my life. ADD, surprisingly?, more so. And recently after chatting with a dear friend of mine, I have come to the realisation, that eventhough I have been taking medication for it for some time now (nearly a decade I think? since my diagnoses at any rate), I'm not finding it... effective or good enough. I take Bupropion, which is in it's essence a anti depressant. And I know that if I don't take it, I AM quite a bit more scatter brained and more high energy to the outside world. However, I have recently realised, I still HAVE all the issues that I had before I took the medication. It's just, only slightly milder. And at the time I accepted that as "well this is the best it'd gon' be". So my aim now is to get back to a psychiatrist, and try out a bunch of other meds that could help, to find the one that I DO find effective enough. And maybe, MAYBE, find one that will actually suppress the ADD enough that I might become the person I really would like to be.

comments.text: We think of our crossed over ones as far away. Nope. I've got a few of these small tap lamps around my living room. Normally I  tap them on the yellow warm light. When I last saw my mom in June last year (she lived at the coast I live inland), it was such an emotionally bonding time between me and my mom. On one occasion I told my mom you know how when a baby is born doctor has to snip the umbilical cord, it would be a bit awkward otherwise. I said well there's another cord, one you can't see, but God created it and runs straight from my soul to yours and nothing can break it. When I got home I hung up a painting from my grandfather's home I've always loved. I remembered I had one of my dad's favourite jerseys (he crossed over when I was 6. He crossed over on Father's Day which to me is a sign he was ready to leave this world). I washed that jersey, bought a great big teddy bear, who now wears my dad's jersey and is sat in a comfy chair looking at that painting that was part of his childhood too. I had two of these touch lamps on a shelf behind him, they're a sort of mushroom shape. Ever since they I put the teddy with his jersey on, these touch lamps would turn on randomly at about 2am. One morning just as I was about to leave for work, I tapped them off and asked out loud dad is it you playing with these lamps at 2am!? Ping the one on the right turned on. I moved them. I love this interview. I’ve seen so many doctors over the years and my most ubiquitous diagnosis combo has been Bipolar 2 and ADHD, which recent therapy has been uncovering could be cPTSD.

I can recall my first major medication reaction was akathisia in response to a mood stabilizer in grade school. I think it was in combination with ritalin but I may have been on adderall by that time. I wound up ripping my clothes off and “climbing the walls” by my parents’ recollection. Dad wound up tossing me out the back door in my underwear because he was exhausted and just wanted to get me to school and go to work.

My late mother’s records have been extremely helpful in identifying and understanding my psych history.

Thanks for sharing this beautiful exchange.

comments.text: I struggled my whole life, assuming that the high demand parenting I had experienced along with constant moving around the country, had caused my mental health issues.  However, from age 2, my parents were told I might have MS as I fainted regularly, went blind in one eye at age 10, had DAILY many multiple events of dizziness and partial  blindness through into my 40s.  Migraines, anxiety, fears, depression.  I had many female problems during that time including surgeries.   I had a partial hysterectomy at 41 and so was unaware that the escalation in symptoms were because it had spontaneously sent me into menopause.  At 50, I figured out that menopause was finished and went to my doctor for a confirmation blood test.  I requested several other tests as well and for some bizarre reason, requested a celiac test.  I discovered I had had celiac disease, my whole life!  No gluten meant dizziness, blindness issues, migraines, etc etc were all reduced dramatically, almost gone!  Even the emotional upheavals decreased!  It was then that I realized that my lovely but sad 12 year old son (who had never slept or ate well at all his whole life and had been mildly suicidal for several years) might be celiac as well!  Got him tested but he was negative.  I read about it and requested a biopsy.  He had the rashes, and many other non tummy issues.   Thank God the biopsy was done by a celiac specialist.  Instead of 1-3 spots taken as most doctors do, he took 15 and said nothing was suspicious until the last 3 spots.  Even then, he wasn't convinced except when he combined all the symptoms and so told us, 'Let's just call him celiac'.  Within 3 months, my son was no longer depressed, ate well and slept!  He is in his mid 20s now and we did get him therapy to unlearn bad thinking he had adopted while sick.  But he is extremely happy, lives across the country from us and is very successful in many ways.  You couldn't pay him, or me, to eat gluten on purpose and we neither one ever had the obvious tummy and bathroom issues!  We love therapy but now it accomplishes goals not just helping us survive that which doesn't seem to have explanation.  Celiac disease causes malnutrition!  Malnutrition affects our brains.  We are evidence of that.

comments.text: The label "treatment resistant depression" is not helpful for the client and, at worst, may cause harm by implying that getting better is hopeless. That said, "treatment resistant depression" is not a diagnosis. It is clinical shorthand for "hey, we've tried these interventions and they didn't work, so we'll need to go off the beaten path to see what's really going on here." While this language may be helpful for progress notes and for clinical consultation among providers, it's not language that should be (or is really meant to be) shared with the client, in my view. It's certainly not language that I would use with a client, at least. But I'm just a counselor in training, so take my opinion with a grain of salt.

Some of us are also hyper sensitive to progesteron (even the bioidentical kind). I am dealing with some hormone imbalances to the extent that my doctor put me on progesterone to try and get things sorted out, and usually progesterone HELPS with sleep. But for me, it woke me up every 15 minutes all night every night I took it and eventually tried taking it during the day which is not generally recommended because it’s supposed to make you sleepy, but we couldn’t think of another option- anyway the result was intense anxiety followed shortly by collapsing very suddenly on the floor unable to move my own limbs. I guess those of us with MTHFR just don’t respond to needed medicine in the usual way…..
I honestly think everyone should get a full MTHFR panel at this point. It seems to be behind a lot of the weird reactions and backwards responses to medication or stimulants. If your liver can’t methylate the help it’s being giving, the help isn’t going to hurt instead of help.

I'm going to lead with something that might sound like an attack (but I promise it isn't):  ADHD isn't real.
ADHD and dyslexia diagnoses are side effects of a collision between population growth, diminishing social value of the trades, and a severely outdated education system.
I don't know you at all, but I can tell that you're probably American from your accent, and probably an aesthete from your grooming style and choice of decor.  Cardboard box in frame is interesting...it's the only thing of its type.  Everything else is perfectly curated.  I would guess that you left it there for effect.
Nothing about you looks like depression.  If you are depressed, why do you exhibit no signs of it?  This isn't me doubting you.  This is me saying, if you are depressed, why are you masking?

You asked a question in response to someone else:  "Is a life worth living without being happy?"  I'm tempted to say "no", just because it breaks the illusion that it's an honest question.  Life's worth is entirely subjective to the individual experience.  If you require "happiness" to a certain level, and you feel your life is not at sufficient "happiness", you have to determine whether a path to the sufficient level exists, right?  This is the trap of depression.

Challenge the parameters.  Are you sure "happiness" is a good metric for determining life's worth?
